standard.title: Develop geographical inquiry questions
standard.description: develop a range of questions for a geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge
standard.prior_knowledge: At Y9, students developed a range of questions for geographical inquiry (AC9HG9S01). At Y10 the added complexity is working with multi-scale phenomena and linking questions across scales (local, national, global) using geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) to sharpen focus.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop a range of relevant questions to investigate a geographical phenomenon or challenge, modifying and refining questions to incorporate geographical concepts and scale of study, and planning an investigation across multiple scales using digital tools.

nodes.label: Generating relevant questions for a geographical phenomenon
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a range of relevant questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or a challenge may arise.
nodes.minimum_width: Generate at least three questions about one geographical phenomenon or challenge, ensuring the questions are geographically relevant (not generic).
nodes.typical_width: Develop a range of relevant questions that together address multiple dimensions of a geographical phenomenon or challenge — covering what, why, where, how and with what consequences; ensuring questions are grounded in geographical concepts.
wider: Develop question sets for two contrasting phenomena (e.g. environmental sustainability and human wellbeing) and compare the inquiry structures, evaluating which questions are most productive for geographical investigation
Investigate how professional geographers frame inquiry questions and compare professional research questions with student-generated questions for the same topic
Generate questions that deliberately cross scales (local, national, global) for the same phenomenon and evaluate how scale change reshapes the inquiry
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot generate questions that are geographically framed rather than generically curious, the entire inquiry they conduct will lack geographical direction — data collection (S02), analysis (S03) and conclusion (S04) all flow from the question quality.

response_modes.reason: Students often generate questions that could apply to any discipline ('What is the problem? How bad is it? What should we do?'). Scaffold geographical question framing explicitly — what makes a question geographical is that it involves place, space, scale, environment or interconnection.

success_criteria: Students generate at least three questions about a phenomenon that are geographically framed, not just generally curious
Students' questions together address multiple aspects of the phenomenon (nature, distribution, causes, consequences, responses)

nodes.label: Refining questions using concepts and scale
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop and modify questions to sharpen the focus of an investigation using geographical concepts and scale of study.
nodes.minimum_width: Take a broad question and modify it to incorporate at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) and a specific scale of study.
nodes.typical_width: Develop and modify a set of inquiry questions so that each incorporates a geographical concept and addresses a specified scale (local, national, global); explain how the concept and scale sharpens the question's focus and what kind of data it calls for.
wider: Develop parallel versions of the same question at three different scales and explain how each version calls for different data, methods and sources
Investigate how geographical concepts function as analytical lenses — taking one concept (e.g. interconnection) and exploring how it reshapes the questions that can be asked about a phenomenon
Evaluate a set of student-generated questions against criteria of focus, researchability and geographical relevance, revising weak questions with explicit justification

response_modes.reason: Practising question refinement across multiple phenomena and concepts builds the transferable skill — students who have only refined questions for one phenomenon may be unable to apply the process to a new topic.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Question refinement using concepts and scales is the core disciplinary thinking skill of geographical inquiry. Students who have practised this across multiple concepts and phenomena develop a more portable inquiry toolkit.
success_criteria: Students modify at least one question to incorporate a named geographical concept, explaining how the concept sharpens the inquiry focus
Students produce a refined question that specifies a scale of study and explain what kind of data that scale requires

nodes.label: Planning a multi-scale investigation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan an investigation of a phenomenon at a range of scales using digital tools.
nodes.minimum_width: Outline a plan for investigating one phenomenon at two or more scales, identifying data sources for each scale.
nodes.typical_width: Plan an investigation of a phenomenon across local, national and/or global scales using digital tools; identify appropriate data sources, methods and questions for each scale; explain how findings at each scale will be integrated.
wider: Plan an investigation that involves both primary data collection (fieldwork, survey) and secondary data sources, specifying how each will be used and how they will be compared
Evaluate a completed geographical investigation plan — identifying strengths and gaps in question coverage, scale consideration and data source selection
Design a digital tool-supported investigation plan for a phenomenon where geospatial technologies (GIS, satellite imagery, interactive mapping) are central to data collection or analysis

response_modes.reason: An investigation plan integrates question development, scale selection and method planning. Students need to see how each question implies a method and data source — the plan is the explicit connection point between inquiry questions and research design.

success_criteria: Students produce an investigation plan that addresses the phenomenon at two or more scales, identifying at least one data source per scale
Students explain how their planned investigation would answer at least two of their refined inquiry questions
